etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English nekke, nakke, from Old English hnecca, *hnæcca (“neck, nape”), from Proto-Germanic *hnakkô (“nape, neck”), from Proto-Indo-European *knog-, *kneg- (“back of the head, nape, neck”). Cognate with Scots nek (“neck”), North Frisian neek, neeke, Nak (“neck”), Saterland Frisian Näkke (“neck”), West Frisian nekke (“neck”), Dutch nek (“neck”), German Low German Nack (“neck”), German Nacken (“nape of the neck”), Danish nakke (“neck”), Swedish nacke (“nape of the neck”), Icelandic hnakki (“neck”), Tocharian A kñuk (“neck, nape”). Possibly a mutated variant of *kneug/k (compare Old English hnocc (“hook, penis”), Welsh cnwch (“joint, knob”), Latvian knaūķis (“dwarf”). Doublet of nek. More at nook. Displaced halse (“neck, throat”) and swire (“neck”).

definitions.definition: (anatomy) The part of the body connecting the head and the trunk found in humans and some animals.

quote.citation: 2019 October 15, ZA/UM, Robert Kurvitz, quoting You, Disco Elysium, →OCLC:
quote.text: Mother, help me, there's a head attached to my neck and I'm in it.

definitions.definition: The corresponding part in some other anatomical contexts.
The part of a shirt, dress etc., which fits a person's neck.
The tapered part of a bottle toward the opening.
(botany) The slender tubelike extension atop an archegonium, through which the sperm swim to reach the egg.

quote.citation: 1992, Rudolf M[athias] Schuster, The Hepaticae and Anthocerotae of North America: East of the Hundredth Meridian, volume V, Chicago, Ill.: Field Museum of Natural History, →ISBN, page 5:
quote.text: Archegonia are surrounded early in their development by the juvenile perianth, through the slender beak of which the elongated neck of the fertilized archegonium protrudes.

definitions.definition: (music) The extension of any stringed instrument on which a fingerboard is mounted
A long narrow tract of land projecting from the main body, or a narrow tract connecting two larger tracts.
(engineering) A reduction in size near the end of an object, formed by a groove around it.
The constriction between the root and crown of a tooth.
(architecture) The gorgerin of a capital.
(geology) A volcanic plug, solidified lava filling the vent of an extinct volcano.
(firearms) The small part of a gun between the chase and the swell of the muzzle.
(figurative) A person's life.
(informal, MLE, slang) A falsehood; a lie.
(slang) Fellatio

quote.text: Shorty throw neck like a geeseShe make me speak Portuguese

quote.citation: 2018, “Florida Thang”, in The South Got Something To Say, performed by Pouya:
quote.text: She drop neck for a check and a paystub

definitions.definition: (now historical) A bundle of wheat used in certain English harvest ceremonies.

quote.citation: 1837, R. A. R., The Everyday Book, page 1169:
quote.text: The person with 'the neck' stands in the centre, grasping it with both his hands

quote.citation: 1911, James George Frazer, The Golden Bough, volume 7, page 266:
quote.text: "The neck" is generally hung up in the farmhouse, where it remains for two or three years.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang) To hang by the neck; strangle; kill, eliminate.
(intransitive, informal, chiefly US) To make love; to intently kiss or cuddle; to canoodle.

quote.citation: 1994 [1993], Irvine Welsh, Trainspotting, London: Minerva, →ISBN, page 326:
quote.text: Molly had been in love with Sick Boy since he necked with her in a seedy disco-bar in Leith a few weeks ago. Sick Boy had made a drunken point about HIV transmission and to illustrate it had spent most of the night french-kissing her.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang) To drink or swallow rapidly.

quote.text: Actually, mostly I swan around in my silver sports car, necking drugs, and feeling sorry for myself.
In the dim light, punters sit sipping raspberry-flavoured Tokyo martinis, losing the freestyle sushi off their chopsticks or necking Asahi beer.

quote.citation: 2019 January 26, Kitty Empire [pseudonym], “The Streets review – the agony and ecstasy of a great everyman”, in Katharine Viner, editor, The Guardian‎[1], London: Guardian News & Media, →ISSN, →OCLC, archived from the original on 8 April 2019:
quote.text: The 40-year-old [Mike Skinner] is happy to put his body on the line in other ways, swapping a mug of tea for a fan's double pint of lager and messily necking it in one.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To decrease in diameter.

quote.citation: 2007, John H. Bickford, Introduction to the Design and Behavior of Bolted Joints, page 272:
quote.text: Since this temperature would place the bolt in its creep range, it will slowly stretch, necking down as it does so. Eventually it will get too thin to support the weight, and the bolt will break.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Danish nøkke, Swedish näck.

definitions.definition: (folklore) A shapeshifting water spirit in Germanic mythology and folklore; a nix.

quote.citation: 1828, Thomas Keightley, The Fairy Mythology, volume I, London: William Harrison Ainsworth, page 234:
quote.text: The Neck no more upon the river sings.And no Mermaid to bleach her linen flingsUpon the waves in the mild solar ray.
